touches.text: Runs a proof as its own process and writes a validation record (claim, caller, date, method, verdict, evidence, falsifier, horizon).
Seals: one current validation per proof, beside the proof. A seal holds while the code it measured is unchanged.

Commit: the proofs of the component the ticket changed, since RULE 1 bounds a change to its component. Passing them puts the component in service, yellow: proven where it changed, not yet measured against what depends on it. In service needs only the best we can do now: 80% trust.
VERBS: run, notices, CodeMother's verbs reached over the bus (RULE 1). COMMANDS: cairn codemother test (--hollow, --seal, --exec, ...), shortcut cairn test; proofgate (the hook: proofs run by hand).

`cairn codemother retire <path>...` does the deletion. It runs the proofs of the files that name the target, before and after moving it aside. A proof that turns red is a caller, and the target goes back. Why? Running a proof tells a caller from a mention; reading the text cannot.

More than one builder runs at a time, so work is kept apart by branches: each ticket's work on its own branch, named by the ticket id, merged locally with git, no pull request (GitHub is hosting only). WHY: branches are how many builders scale.

Outline check: when a ticket is cast, the cheapest model reads it beside the outline sections it touches. A conflict, or an open question in those sections, becomes a [Q#n] at the outline line it bears on (0.6.2), and that open [Q#n] holds the ticket's build until it is answered. It reads the outline as it stands each time, so editing the outline costs nothing. WHY: a ticket that contradicts the outline builds something Akien did not intend, and the cheapest time to catch that is before the build. - CC
Test runs are transient (30 days, 4.3.2); seals are records of truth (git).
Test tiers: commit, hourly, daily and weekly. Each tier runs only what it must, so a commit needs only its own proofs and the long runs wait for the long tiers; nothing runs just in case.

Reds don't get lost. Each run writes a ticket for every new red it finds and every orphaned file it sees, unless one is already open for it. A red seen in passing gets the same treatment. Every red and every orphaned file is fixed; one unrelated to the work in hand is ticketed, and once it is, that crossing can go ahead.
TOOLS: base, validation_store, proof_coverage, scratch, question, proof_discovery, chain, bus_client, artifact, system_word; machine build_inspector; db client.

The seal is checked where the proof runs, not in the command's text: a proof refuses to run outside the tester's seal, so no spelling reaches the live ~/.cairn. proofgate only rewrites the common spelling for convenience. CC's decision, Q#101.
A proof that cannot go red without its build (its hollow is empty) stands only on Akien's answered approval, recorded as the hollow reading and re-read at clearance; any other empty hollow is red.
import_sieve: one parse of every .py into an import graph; what reaches what. WHY: enforces "only the proxy reaches the host/database" and RULE 1 by physics. USERS: CodeMother, the inference proxy.

conflicts.ticket_says: In proofs_touching, unsealed staged proofs are added to the result, so reseal_all runs them and stages their first seal.
conflicts.why: 9.4.2.3.7.5 states 'Reds don't get lost. Each run writes a ticket for every new red it finds...'. A newly added proof sealed red-first is a new red from the tester run, but the ticket description specifies only that the seal is staged, with no mention of ticket creation. The bounds note the hook script ruling is a separate ticket, but the clause 'Each run writes a ticket for every new red' would not demonstrably hold after the ticket is built as written unless ticket creation is explicitly ensured by the same change. The ticket's how-clause must state whether a ticket is created or explain why this red is exempt from 9.4.2.3.7.5's requirement.
